title: ‘Umrat al-Qada’ • Mu’tah • The Three Hundred at the Seashore • Final Word

blocks.1: A year came around. In the month of Dhu al-Qa‘dah of the seventh year of Hijrah, the Prophet {{1}} went to Makkah to perform ‘umrah in accordance with the terms of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah. This ‘umrah is called ‘Umrat al-Qada’. All who had been at Hudaybiyah, the Prophet {{2}} asked to come along. Except those who had been martyred in the meantime, no one stayed behind. Two thousand people, not counting women and children. This time they did not enter with weapons. At a place called Yajaj they left all their arms under the guard of two hundred men. With them there was only the sheathed sword, just as it was written in the treaty.{{3}}
blocks.2: The polytheists of Makkah were looking from the direction of the mountain. They were saying among themselves, the fever of Yathrib has weakened them. The Prophet {{1}} said to the Companions, walk fast in the first three rounds, swaying the shoulders, so that the polytheists see your strength.{{2}}
blocks.3: That fast walk of the tawaf the pilgrims still do today. What began one day as the answer to an accusation of weakness remained a Sunnah until the Day of Resurrection. Showing the believer’s firmness too sometimes becomes worship. Ibn ‘Abbas (RA) said, the Prophet {{1}} did not tell the Companions to do ramal in all the rounds, only out of compassion for them. Showing strength in the first three rounds, walking normally in the remaining four.{{2}}
blocks.4: The one at whose command the Companions would give their lives saw how tired the Companions were. Even inside the command to show strength there was a reckoning of capacity. ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA) was walking ahead of the Prophet {{1}} reciting verses, addressing the disbelievers: clear the way. ‘Umar (RA) said, Ibn Rawahah, in front of the Messenger of Allah {{2}}, in Allah’s Haram, poetry? The Prophet {{3}} said, ‘Umar, let him be; his words reach them faster than arrows.{{4}}
blocks.5: A year earlier ‘Umar (RA) had asked, did you not say we would go to the Ka‘bah and perform tawaf? That day the answer had come, did I say, this very year? Today is that tawaf. The Qur’an had told of this promise beforehand in this way,
blocks.7: In fact Allah had shown His Messenger a true dream, which was entirely in accordance with reality. You will surely enter the Masjid al-Haram in safety, in such a state that (some of) you will have your heads shaved and (some) will have hair cut short, without fear. Allah knows what you do not know. So before that dream is fulfilled He has ordained an imminent victory.{{1}}
blocks.8: The dream was true, the timing was Allah’s to set. In between came Khaybar, that imminent victory. A promise that is fulfilled late is not a forgotten promise. In history this ‘umrah is found with four names: Qada’, Qadiyyah, Qisas and Sulh, that is, peace treaty. The treaty about which the Companions had so many questions in their hearts, its very name became one name of this ‘umrah.{{1}}
blocks.10: The three days were completed. Quraysh sent a man to ‘Ali (RA): tell your companion, time is up, let him leave. The Prophet {{1}} set out. From behind a small girl came running, calling, uncle, uncle. Hamzah’s (RA) daughter; her father had been martyred at Uhud, she had stayed behind in Makkah. ‘Ali (RA) took her hand and said to Fatimah (RA), take her, your uncle’s daughter. Then there was a tug-of-war over the girl among three people. ‘Ali (RA) said, I have more right, she is my uncle’s daughter. Ja‘far (RA) said, she is my uncle’s daughter too, and her maternal aunt is my wife. Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) said, she is my brother’s daughter. The Prophet {{2}} gave the girl to her maternal aunt. He said,
blocks.12: A maternal aunt is in the position of a mother. To ‘Ali he said, you are from me and I am from you. To Ja‘far he said, you resemble me in appearance and in character. To Zayd he said, you are our brother, our mawla.{{1}}
blocks.13: Three people quarrelling to keep one orphan girl with them. And in giving the judgement the Prophet {{1}} said to all three such words as they kept in their hearts for life. The ruling went for one, and no one’s heart was broken.
blocks.14: Two of those three that day, Zayd and Ja‘far, would be martyred together on one battlefield only a few months later.
blocks.16: Jumada al-Ula of the eighth year of Hijrah. The Prophet {{1}} had sent al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi (RA) with a letter to the ruler of Busra. On the way near Mu’tah, the Ghassanid ruler loyal to Rome, Shurahbil ibn ‘Amr, bound him and killed him. Killing an envoy was, even in those days, the greatest insult.{{2}}
blocks.17: The Prophet {{1}} sent an army of three thousand. He appointed Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) as commander. He said, if Zayd is martyred then Ja‘far; if Ja‘far is martyred then ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah.{{2}}
blocks.18: On the day of departure everyone gathered to see off the commanders. In that crowd ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA) was weeping. The people asked, why are you weeping? He said, by Allah, I am not weeping out of love of the world or love for you. I heard the Prophet {{1}} recite a verse of the Qur’an which says everyone must pass over Hell. I do not know what will happen to me then. The people said, may Allah keep you safe, ward off every danger, bring you back to us victorious. He said,
blocks.20: But I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness, and ask for a sword-blow that will tear apart the liver and the entrails. Then the traveller will pass by the grave and say, a fighter in the way of Allah, Allah has guided him, he has indeed been guided.{{1}}
blocks.21: Then the army set out. The Prophet {{1}} walked with them as far as Thaniyyat al-Wada‘. Standing there he gave the final farewell.{{2}}
blocks.22: This man is going on, asking for martyrdom, yet his weeping is from fear of accountability. Courage and weeping can be in the same heart. One who does not fear has perhaps not understood anything; one who fears yet goes forward, that one is the brave. Reaching the border of Sham, news came: ahead, a huge army of Rome, with Arab tribes along. Some said, let us write to the Prophet {{1}}, either he will send more men or give other instructions. ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA) stood up and said, the very thing you now dislike, martyrdom, is what you came out to seek. We do not fight with numbers or strength; we fight with this religion by which Allah has honoured us. One of the two good things will surely be had: victory, or else martyrdom.{{2}}
blocks.24: The battle began. First of all Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) took up the banner. Sword in hand he fought as few have in all of history. At one point, riddled by the enemy’s spears, he fell; he was martyred. Before the banner could fall to the ground Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib (RA) took it up. He dismounted from his own reddish horse and cut the horse’s legs. He kept fighting. At one point his right hand was cut off and fell. He took the banner in his left hand. A little later the left hand too was gone. Then, pressing the banner between his two arms, he held it high. Thus he was martyred. Then ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA) took up the banner. He was on horseback. There was a little hesitation in his heart. He said to himself,
blocks.26: O my nafs! I swear to you, come down onto the battlefield, whether you wish it or not. If others keep the war stirred up and level their spears, why do I see only you sitting away from Paradise?{{1}}
blocks.28: Then he dismounted from the horse. His cousin brought a bone with meat on it and said, brother, strengthen your back with this, a hard day has gone over you today. He took the bone in his hand and bit it once. Then he threw it away and went forward sword in hand. Fighting on, he was martyred. This dialogue with one’s own nafs is familiar to all of us. The heart says, I’ll do this later, let me rest a little now. Ibn Rawahah scolded himself. The bite of the bone was not to satisfy hunger, but to throw off even the thought of how weak the body had grown. Later Ibn ‘Umar (RA) stood by Ja‘far’s body and counted the wounds; fifty blows of spear and sword, not one on the back.{{1}}
blocks.29: When later Ibn ‘Umar (RA) met Ja‘far’s son, he would greet him thus: peace be upon you, O son of the one with two wings.{{1}}
blocks.30: The One Who Gave the News from Madinah
blocks.31: The news from Mu’tah had not yet reached Madinah. The Prophet {{1}} stood before the people and gave the news,
blocks.33: Zayd took the banner, he was martyred. Then Ja‘far took it, he was martyred. Then Ibn Rawahah took it, he was martyred.{{1}}
blocks.34: As he spoke, tears were flowing from his two eyes. Then he said, finally one of the swords of Allah took up the banner, and Allah gave them victory. That sword of Allah was Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA); only a few months earlier he had accepted Islam. He used to say, on the day of Mu’tah nine swords broke in my hand; in the end only a Yemeni broad sword remained in my hand.{{1}}
blocks.35: Thabit ibn Aqram (RA) of Banu ‘Ajlan took up the fallen banner and said, choose one from among yourselves as commander. The people said, you be it. He said, I cannot. Then everyone chose Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA). On the first day, all day, he stood firm before that vast army. He understood that now a strategy was needed by which the Muslims could slowly withdraw from the field, yet the enemy would not get a chance to pursue. If they ran scattered, the Romans would pursue and finish everyone. On the morning of the second day Khalid rearranged the army. He took the front rows to the back, the back rows to the front. The right wing to the left, the left wing to the right. Coming forward, the Romans saw new faces, new banners. They said to one another, help has come to the Muslims from Madinah. A little after the fighting began, Khalid (RA) slowly began to fold the lines and retreat. The army’s discipline was intact. The Romans thought, this is a trap of the Muslims; a strategy to pull them into the desert and finish them. They did not pursue. The Muslim army returned safely to Madinah. Twelve Muslims were martyred in this battle. How many casualties the Romans had is not known. All that is known is that a small band of three thousand returned from before two hundred thousand.{{1}}
blocks.36: Pulling back is sometimes winning. It is because they have the courage to return with everything intact that some are able to stop at the right time. We are afraid to stop, because we count stopping as defeat. After this battle the Arab tribes such as Banu Sulaym, Ashja‘, Ghatafan, Dhubyan and Fazarah, who had been deadly enemies of the Muslims, came one by one and took shelter in the shade of Islam. Mu’tah opened their eyes: those who have this faith with them are not defeated by numbers.{{1}}
blocks.37: Of the three who only a few months earlier had been quarrelling to keep an orphan girl, two of them, and that Ibn Rawahah in whose hand the measure of Khaybar’s crop had been that day, all three went away on one day, on one battlefield. And far away, the one who bade each of them farewell by name, his eyes grew wet.
blocks.38: We think, there is time; I’ll call later, I’ll meet later. The joy the Prophet {{1}} felt at getting Ja‘far back after thirteen years, it took less than a year to lose that same Ja‘far again.
blocks.39: The Three Hundred at the Seashore
blocks.40: Around the time of Mu’tah the Prophet {{1}} sent another small army toward the coast of the sea. Three hundred men, commander Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA). The aim was to block the route of a trade caravan of Quraysh. On the way the food ran low. Abu ‘Ubaydah (RA) told everyone to collect their provisions. Two bags of dates were collected. Every day a little at a time was given to everyone from it. At last a day came when one date per head fell to each. Jabir (RA) was later asked by a student, what can one date do? He said,
blocks.42: When they ran out we felt their lack.{{1}}
blocks.44: Then they reached the edge of the sea. They saw a huge fish lying like a hill. Three hundred men ate from that fish and passed eighteen nights. Abu ‘Ubaydah had two of its ribs set up. A she-camel was saddled and passed under them. It did not touch the ribs. The very army that felt the lack of the date because it had run out, one day got food like a mountain. We often understand the value of a blessing in hand only after losing it. Those who know the price of one date are more thankful for a full meal too. And the army’s commander, the same man, in the days of hunger ate sharing with everyone. He did not keep a separate bag for himself. A leader who shares even the last date with all, people go with him even to the edge of the sea.
blocks.46: From Khaybar to Mu’tah, a few pictures of these year and a half remain in the mind. Ears attentive, waiting for an adhan even on a night of war. The announcement of two rewards for ‘Amir, martyred by his own sword. Ibn Rawahah’s measure, returning the jewellery of the bribe, full justice even with someone he disliked. The poisoned goat and one ‘no’, whose pain he carried for four years. Salamah, who ran alone at Dhu Qarad and brought back all the camels, whom the Prophet {{1}} seated behind him. Bilal, who fell asleep at the time of prayer on the way back, and, with no rebuke, only the next thing to do. The three hundred at the seashore who felt the lack of one date. And Ibn Rawahah’s scolding of his own nafs. The kiss on Ja‘far’s forehead; being unable to decide which was greater, the conquest of Khaybar or the return of a brother. The good news of two hijrahs for the boat people who had been far away. The sweet quarrel of three guardians over Hamzah’s daughter. And the two eyes that grew wet in giving the news of Mu’tah. The brothers with whom one day we walked shoulder to shoulder, they are still there today, but there is no talk. So take away one deed from today’s dars.
blocks.48: When Ja‘far (RA) returned the Prophet {{1}} had said, I cannot tell whether I am happier at the conquest of Khaybar or at Ja‘far’s coming. Today I will ask myself a question: how many brothers in faith were there with whom I no longer speak; is the reason really busyness, or something else? Today I will phone a brother with whom there has been no contact for a long time, and truly want to know how he is; I will not give up this checking in from today.

footnotes.0: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 623 (Fath al-Bari 7/500; Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma‘ad 2/151): Imam al-Hakim says, it is established through several mutawatir chains that, on seeing the crescent of Dhu al-Qa‘dah, the Prophet {{1}} told those who had been at Hudaybiyah to go with him; except those already martyred everyone set out, with some others also; the number two thousand, not counting women and children. The arms were left at Yajaj, with two hundred men guarding, and Aws ibn Khawli al-Ansari (RA) given the charge; they entered Makkah with only the sheathed sword. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence. The condition of the sheathed sword was in the treaty itself, Sahih al-Bukhari 2699, 4251.
footnotes.1: Sahih al-Bukhari 1602 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (RA); the polytheists’ ‘the fever of Yathrib has weakened them’ and the instruction of ramal in the first three rounds). The polytheists were watching from the direction of the Qu‘ayqi‘an mountain, in Sahih Muslim 1266.
footnotes.2: Sahih al-Bukhari 1602, 4256; Sahih Muslim 1266 (‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (RA)): ‘The Prophet {{1}} did not command them to do ramal in all the rounds, only out of compassion (ibqa’).’ Ahmad Shakir: the chain is sahih. Staying three days: Sunan Abi Dawud 1997 (from Ibn ‘Abbas: ‘the Prophet {{2}} stayed three days at the ‘Umrat al-Qada’’; al-Albani: sahih).
footnotes.3: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 2847 (from Anas (RA)); Imam al-Tirmidhi: hasan sahih gharib. Ibn Hajar (Ithaf al-Mahara): on the condition of al-Bukhari, though al-Bukhari did not bring it with a connected chain. The first line of Ibn Rawahah’s poem: ‘O sons of the disbeliever, clear his path.’
footnotes.4: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 3, Surah al-Fath 48:27, p. 378 (Taqi ‘Uthmani, checked by rendering the PDF). Note 29: before Hudaybiyah the Prophet {{1}} had seen in a dream that he had entered the Masjid al-Haram with the Companions; on having to return without ‘umrah, questions arose in some hearts; the verse told that the dream was true, but the time was not fixed; the next year it was fulfilled. Note 30: the ‘imminent victory’ is Khaybar.
footnotes.5: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 630 (Fath al-Bari 7/500): the four names of this ‘umrah: Qada’, Qadiyyah, Qisas, Sulh (peace treaty). Two reasons for the name ‘Qada’’: the making-up (qada’) of the ‘umrah of Hudaybiyah, or according to the settlement of the treaty (in the sense of ‘taqada’); to researchers the second is more acceptable. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 2699 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); Quraysh’s ‘time is up’ message, the ‘uncle, uncle’ call of Hamzah’s (RA) daughter, the claims of ‘Ali, Ja‘far and Zayd, ‘a maternal aunt is in the position of a mother’ and the three sayings to the three). Ja‘far (RA)’s wife Asma’ bint ‘Umays was the girl’s maternal aunt. Zayd (RA) said ‘my brother’s daughter’ because in Madinah the Prophet {{1}} had made a brotherhood between him and Hamzah (RA) (Ibn Sa‘d, Sirah-based). ‘Mawla’ here means a freed close one.
footnotes.7: Al-Waqidi, al-Maghazi ← Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, ‘Ghazwat Mu’tah’ (the killing of al-Harith ibn ‘Umayr al-Azdi (RA)). Sirah-based; this incident has not come in the sahih hadith books as the cause of Mu’tah, so it is given as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.8: Sahih al-Bukhari 4261 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Umar (RA); the order of the three commanders). The number of the army, three thousand, is in the narration of Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham.
footnotes.10: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 633 (Ibn Hisham 2/373–374; Zad al-Ma‘ad 2/156): ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA)’s weeping, the verse that says everyone must pass over Hell (Surah Maryam 19:71) and his poem; the Prophet {{1}} accompanied them to Thaniyyat al-Wada‘ and bade farewell. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.11: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, ‘Ghazwat Mu’tah’ (the consultation at a place called Ma‘an and the speech of ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA)). Sirah-based. The huge number that Ibn Ishaq mentioned for the size of the Roman army, because it did not come through a verifiable chain, no number has been given in the dars.
footnotes.13: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 635–637 (Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham 2/375–376; Zad al-Ma‘ad 2/156): Zayd’s advancing with the banner and martyrdom by spear; Ja‘far’s dismounting from the horse and cutting its legs, taking the banner in the left hand when the right hand was cut off, pressing it between the two arms when the left was gone; Ibn Rawahah’s hesitation and poem, the cousin’s bringing a bone with meat. In the sahih chains of Bukhari 4262, 3709, 4264 only this much is found: the three commanders were martyred, Ja‘far ‘with two wings’. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 4260 (Nafi‘ ← Ibn ‘Umar (RA): fifty blows of spear and sword, not one on the back). In another narration of the same Companion (Bukhari 4261) more than ninety, counting spear and arrow. The scholars’ reconciliation: in one only the spear and sword blows on the front side are counted, in the other everything including arrows.
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 3709, 4264 (al-Sha‘bi ← Ibn ‘Umar (RA)). As the source of ‘two wings’, the narration in Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 3763: ‘I saw Ja‘far flying in Paradise with the angels.’ Imam al-Tirmidhi called it gharib (Ibn Ma‘in called the narrator ‘Abdullah ibn Ja‘far weak); al-Albani called it sahih on the basis of supporting narrations.
footnotes.16: Sahih al-Bukhari 4262 (from Anas (RA); giving the news of the three martyrs to the people before the news had arrived). The same hadith is in Bukhari 3757 too.
footnotes.17: Sahih al-Bukhari 4262 (‘wa ‘aynahu tadhrifan’, ‘sayf min suyufillah’); Sahih al-Bukhari 4265, 4266 (Qays ibn Abi Hazim ← Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA): nine swords broke, one Yemeni broad sword remained in hand). Khalid (RA)’s acceptance of Islam was in Safar of 8 AH; ‘a few months earlier’ is a calculation.
footnotes.18: Sahih al-Bukhari 4262 (Anas (RA)): ‘Then Khalid ibn al-Walid took the banner, he had not been made commander; Allah gave victory at his hand’. Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 637–639 (Ibn Ishaq; Ibn Hisham 2/376–378; Zad al-Ma‘ad 2/156; Fath al-Bari 7/513–514): Thabit ibn Aqram (RA) took up the banner and asked everyone to choose one, on his saying he could not everyone chose Khalid; Khalid’s changing of the ranks on the morning of the second day (front rank to the back, right to left, left to right); the enemy’s belief that help had come from Madinah; then slowly withdrawing, the Romans thinking it a trap. About the last part of the battle al-Rahiq itself speaks of disagreement: ‘this much is the essence after seeing all the narrations’. Muslim martyrs twelve; Roman casualties not known. This part is Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.19: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 640 (the result of the battle of Mu’tah): after Mu’tah Banu Sulaym, Ashja‘, Ghatafan, Dhubyan and Fazarah quickly came to Islam. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.20: Sahih al-Bukhari 4360, 4361; Sahih Muslim 1935 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA); sahih): The Prophet {{1}} sent an army of three hundred toward the coast, commander Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA); when provisions ran out everyone’s provisions were collected and became two bags of dates, a little each day; at last one date per head. The student Wahb ibn Kaysan asked, what can one date do? Jabir (RA) said, ‘When they ran out we felt their lack.’ Then at the edge of the sea a huge fish like a hill; they ate for eighteen nights; Abu ‘Ubaydah had two of its ribs set up, the camel passed under them, it did not touch the rib. Time of the event: al-Bukhari brought it in the ‘Maghazi’ section after the incident of Mu’tah; there is disagreement among Sirah scholars about year and month, so it has not been fixed in the dars. In this dars the rest of the fish account (informing the Prophet {{2}} after the army returned, giving something to the Prophet {{3}} too) has been left out.
footnotes.21: Sahih al-Bukhari 4360, 4361; Sahih Muslim 1935 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA); sahih): The Prophet {{1}} sent an army of three hundred toward the coast, commander Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA); when provisions ran out everyone’s provisions were collected and became two bags of dates, a little each day; at last one date per head. quiz.q: Why was the instruction to walk fast in the first three rounds given in ‘Umrat al-Qada’?
o: To finish the tawaf quickly
To escape the heat
To show the polytheists strength
To avoid the crowd
quiz.e: The polytheists were saying the fever of Yathrib had weakened them.

quiz.q: Who was reciting verses ahead of the Prophet ﷺ in ‘Umrat al-Qada’?
o: ‘Amir ibn al-Akwa‘
Hassan ibn Thabit al-Ansari
Ka‘b ibn Zuhayr
‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah
quiz.e: ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah (RA).

quiz.q: To whom did the Prophet ﷺ give Hamzah’s (RA) daughter?
o: Her maternal aunt
Fatimah (RA)
Zayd’s wife
He kept her in his own house
quiz.e: A maternal aunt is in the position of a mother.

quiz.q: What is the lesson of ramal, begun in answer to an accusation of weakness, remaining a Sunnah?
o: Answering accusations is always necessary
Walking fast in tawaf is best
Imitating the polytheists is permissible
Showing the believer’s firmness too becomes worship
quiz.e: A deed of the moment of need became a Sunnah until the Day of Resurrection.

quiz.q: How is Surah al-Fath 48:27 connected to ‘Umrat al-Qada’?
o: The dream was true, the time was set by Allah
The verse was revealed after ‘Umrat al-Qada’
The verse forbids ‘umrah
The verse is in fact a direct order for the battle of Khaybar
quiz.e: The dream of Hudaybiyah was fulfilled the next year.

quiz.q: What is the characteristic of the Prophet’s ﷺ ruling in the case of Hamzah’s daughter?
o: He divided her equally among all three
The ruling went for one, and no one’s heart was broken
He postponed the ruling
He returned the girl to Quraysh in Makkah
quiz.e: To all three he said words which they remembered all their lives.

quiz.q: Something you asked of Allah is coming late; what comfort does the incident of ‘Umrat al-Qada’ give?
o: Delay means rejection
It is better to stop asking
Everything should happen in one’s own time
Delay does not mean forgetting
quiz.e: The dream was true, and it was fulfilled the next year.

quiz.q: Two children are quarrelling and a ruling must go in favour of one; what can be taken from the Prophet’s ﷺ method?
o: Keeping everyone’s heart along with the ruling
Ruling in favour of the elder
Giving no ruling and leaving the matter
Scolding both equally
quiz.e: To all three he spoke separate words of love.

quiz.q: No one in the family is coming forward to take responsibility for an orphaned relative; which scene of this dars shows the opposite picture?
o: The takbir announcement on the morning of Khaybar
The tug-of-war of three over Hamzah’s daughter
Abu Musa’s boat journey
Appointing three commanders in succession for Mu’tah
quiz.e: Three people competing to keep an orphan girl.

quiz.q: In a gathering someone’s verse or speech is shaking the opponent in favour of the religion, yet someone raises an objection; what was the Prophet’s ﷺ position?
o: Always stopping all poetry
Silencing the objector and sending him away
Adjourning the gathering and walking out
Letting the speech of good purpose go on
quiz.e: He said, ‘Umar, let him be; his words hit faster than arrows.

quiz.q: Who was the first commander at Mu’tah?
o: Ja‘far ibn Abi Talib
Zayd ibn Harithah
‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah
Khalid ibn al-Walid
quiz.e: Zayd, then Ja‘far, then Ibn Rawahah.

quiz.q: How many swords broke in Khalid’s (RA) hand on the day of Mu’tah?
o: Three
Seven
Nine
Twelve
quiz.e: Nine; in the end one Yemeni sword remained.

quiz.q: What did Thabit ibn Aqram (RA) do on taking up the fallen banner at Mu’tah?
o: Cut the legs of his own horse
Threw away the bone and took up the sword
Told everyone to choose one
Repelled them by throwing stones from the mountain
quiz.e: Everyone chose Khalid; this is Sirah-based.

quiz.q: What is the essence of ‘Abdullah ibn Rawahah’s (RA) speech at Mu’tah?
o: To go back and bring more soldiers
To quickly make peace with the enemy
Fighting with the religion, not with numbers
To leave the fight and wait
quiz.e: One of the two good things will surely be had: victory, or else martyrdom.

quiz.q: What is the meaning of none of Ja‘far’s (RA) wounds being on the back?
o: He was wearing armour
The enemy never got a chance to attack from behind
He did not enter the fight
He did not retreat; he fought from the front
quiz.e: All the wounds were on the front side.

quiz.q: Before the news arrived, the Prophet ﷺ announced the three martyrs; which detail came with it?
o: His two eyes were shedding tears
He told everyone not to leave Madinah
He sent a new army
He told them to observe three days of mourning
quiz.e: ‘Wa ‘aynahu tadhrifan’: his two eyes were flowing with water.

quiz.q: Who is meant by ‘one of the swords of Allah’?
o: ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib
Khalid ibn al-Walid
Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam
Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib
quiz.e: The one who finally took up the banner and brought victory.

quiz.q: What does the incident of Ibn Rawahah (RA) scolding his own nafs and descending to the battlefield teach?
o: The right of those far away does not diminish
Justice even with those one dislikes
Not passing judgement by outward appearance
Going against what the heart wants
quiz.e: In the poem he made himself swear and come down.

quiz.q: Seeing a huge obstacle ahead in a task, everyone in the team wants to fall back; what can be taken from Ibn Rawahah’s words?
o: Turning back on seeing an obstacle is wise
No work unless everyone agrees
Not numbers, but intention and ideal are the strength
First gathering more people is essential
quiz.e: We do not fight with numbers.

quiz.q: Tears come to the eyes while giving news of the death of a loved one; what does the Prophet’s ﷺ practice say?
o: Expressing grief is always forbidden
Weeping is a sign of weakness
The news should be given through someone else
Tears are not opposed to patience
quiz.e: His eyes grew wet in giving the news of the three martyrs.

quiz.q: Two of the Companions who had been seen together only a few months earlier were both martyred at Mu’tah; what realisation arises?
o: Going to war should be avoided
Checking on relationships: not later, now
Counting the number of martyrs is necessary
Forgetting old relationships is best
quiz.e: The one I can check on today, perhaps tomorrow I cannot.

quiz.q: Who was the commander of the army of three hundred sent toward the seashore?
o: Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) (commander of Mu’tah)
Abu ‘Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah (RA)
Khalid ibn al-Walid (RA)
Thabit ibn Aqram (RA)
quiz.e: Bukhari 4360.

quiz.q: Which is the example of understanding the value of a blessing in hand only after losing it?
o: Ja‘far’s returning to Madinah
The martyrdom of three commanders in one day
Feeling the lack of one date
Three guardians over Hamzah’s daughter
quiz.e: ‘When they ran out we felt it’; Bukhari 4360.

quiz.q: According to the final practical resolve of the dars, what is today’s task?
o: Phoning a brother with whom there has been no talk for a long time
Taking on the responsibility of an orphan
Returning an offer of a bribe
Practising ramal in tawaf
quiz.e: Checking on a brother with whom there is no contact.
